questions.question: A linear program $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ has at least one feasible solution, and $Z$ is bounded above on its feasible region. What can be concluded about its optimal solutions?
options: An optimal solution exists only if the feasible region is also bounded.
At least one optimal solution exists, so the maximum of $Z$ is attained.
The supremum of $Z$ is finite but may be approached without being attained.
Exactly one optimal solution exists, and it is a feasible corner point.

questions.question: For a linear program, which list contains every possible number of optimal solutions and no impossible one?
options: $0$, $1$, $2$, and so on, up to the number of feasible corner points
$0$ or $1$, since every optimal solution is a corner point
$1$ or infinitely many, since every linear program has an optimum
$0$, $1$ or infinitely many, but never a finite number above $1$

questions.question: A linear program has $n$ variables; $\boldsymbol{A}$ is the coefficient matrix of its constraints, and $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}$ that of the constraints together with the domain definitions (lower bounds such as $x_j\geq0$). When does it have at least one corner point?
options: If and only if $\operatorname{rank}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}})=n$
If and only if $\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{A})=n$
If and only if its feasible region is bounded
If and only if $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}$ has at least $n$ rows

questions.question: A linear program in standard form, $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, has a nonempty but unbounded feasible region. Which outcomes are possible, depending on $\boldsymbol{c}$?
options: Only an unbounded objective, since $Z$ grows along some direction of the region
Unbounded or infinitely many optimal solutions, but never exactly one
Unbounded, exactly one optimal solution, or infinitely many optimal solutions
An optimal solution exactly when every entry of $\boldsymbol{c}$ is at most $0$

questions.question: A linear program $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ has a nonempty and bounded feasible region. Which statement about its optimal solutions holds for every objective vector $\boldsymbol{c}$?
options: There is exactly one optimal solution, and it is a corner point.
There is exactly one or there are infinitely many optimal solutions.
There is an optimal solution only if $\boldsymbol{c}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$.
The linear program can still be unbounded if the entries of $\boldsymbol{c}$ are large.

questions.question: Classify the linear program: maximize $Z=2x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\geq5$, $x_1+2x_2\leq4$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$. Is it infeasible, unbounded, or does it have an optimal solution?
options: It is unbounded: $x_1$ can grow without limit while $x_1+x_2\geq5$ holds.
It has the unique optimal solution $(4,0)$, with $Z=8$.
It is infeasible: no $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ satisfies both constraints.
Its optimum is where both constraint lines meet, $(6,-1)$, with $Z=11$.

questions.question: Maximize $Z=x_1-x_2$ subject to $-x_1+x_2\leq2$, $x_1-2x_2\leq3$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$. Which outcome does this linear program have, and which feasible points show it?
options: It has the unique optimal solution $(3,0)$, with $Z=3$.
It is unbounded: the feasible points $(\lambda,2+\lambda)$, $\lambda\geq0$, leave every bounded set.
It is unbounded: the feasible points $(3+2\lambda,\lambda)$, $\lambda\geq0$, have $Z=3+\lambda$.
It has infinitely many optimal solutions with $Z=3$, on the edge where $x_1-2x_2=3$.

questions.question: For the linear program maximize $Z=-x_1+2x_2$ subject to $-x_1+2x_2\leq4$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$, which statement about the objective and the optimal solutions is correct?
options: Infinitely many optima with $Z=4$, such as $(2\lambda,2+\lambda)$, $\lambda\geq0$
Unbounded, since feasible points with arbitrarily large $x_1,x_2$ exist
Exactly one optimum, the feasible corner point $(0,2)$, with $Z=4$
No optimum, since a linear program cannot have an unbounded optimal set

questions.question: A linear program has the zero objective: maximize $Z=0x_1+0x_2$ subject to $x_1+3x_2\leq6$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$. How many optimal solutions does it have?
options: Exactly one, the corner point $(0,0)$, where $Z=0$
Exactly three, the feasible corner points $(0,0)$, $(6,0)$ and $(0,2)$
None, because an objective with $\boldsymbol{c}=\boldsymbol{0}$ has no maximum
Infinitely many, because every feasible point is optimal

questions.question: In the linear program maximize $Z=5x_1-3x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq0$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$, the only constraint has right-hand side $0$. How many optimal solutions are there?
options: None: no point with $x_1,x_2\geq0$ satisfies $x_1+x_2\leq0$.
Exactly one, $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}$, with optimal value $Z=0$.
None: $Z$ is unbounded, because the coefficient $5$ of $x_1$ is positive.
Infinitely many, all on the line $x_1+x_2=0$, with $Z=0$.

questions.question: A linear program in standard form, $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, is known to have a feasible solution. Which statement is then guaranteed?
options: It has a feasible corner point, that is, an extreme point of the feasible region.
It has an optimal solution, attained at a feasible corner point.
The origin $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}$ is feasible, so it is a feasible corner point.
Every corner point, a point where $n$ independent constraints bind, is feasible.

questions.question: A linear program in variables $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ has the constraints $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$, domain definitions included, and a nonempty bounded feasible region. Which statement about $\operatorname{rank}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}})$ is correct?
options: It may be below $n$, since a bounded region can be cut out by constraints without any corner point.
It is $n$, but every corner point may still be infeasible, so the region need not contain one.
It equals the number of rows of $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}$, since a bounded region needs every constraint.
It is $n$, since with a smaller rank the feasible region would contain a whole line through each of its points.

questions.question: A linear program $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ in free variables $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ has constraints $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ with $\operatorname{rank}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}})<n$, and $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is an optimal solution. Why is $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ not the only optimal solution?
options: The feasible region is then unbounded, and on an unbounded feasible region an optimal solution is never unique.
Some $\boldsymbol{d}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ has $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{0}$, and then $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{d}=0$ holds for every $\boldsymbol{c}\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

Some $\boldsymbol{d}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ has $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{0}$; the line $\boldsymbol{x}^*+\lambda\boldsymbol{d}$ is feasible, so $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{d}=0$.
Without a corner point an optimal solution lies where no constraint is binding, and such points always form an open set.

questions.question: Maximize $Z=x_1+x_2+x_3$ subject to $x_1+x_2+x_3\leq4$, $x_1-x_2\leq1$, $2x_1+x_3\leq5$, with $x_1,x_2,x_3\in\mathbb{R}$ and no domain definitions; $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}$ is the $3\times3$ constraint matrix. Which description of this linear program is correct?
options: $\operatorname{rank}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}})=2$, no corner point, and infinitely many optimal solutions with $Z=4$
$\operatorname{rank}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}})=3$, and a unique optimum where all three constraints bind, with $Z=4$
It is unbounded, because the free variables $x_1,x_2,x_3$ can be made as large as desired
$\operatorname{rank}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}})=2$, no corner point, and therefore no optimal solution at all

questions.question: Maximize $Z=3x_1+6x_2$ subject to $x_1+2x_2\leq8$, $x_1\leq4$, $x_2\leq3$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$. How many optimal solutions does this linear program have, and what is the optimal value?
options: Exactly two, the corner points $(4,2)$ and $(2,3)$, with $Z=24$
Infinitely many, the segment from $(4,2)$ to $(2,3)$, with $Z=24$
Exactly one, the corner point $(4,3)$ where both bounds bind, with $Z=30$
Infinitely many, the whole segment of $x_1+2x_2=8$ between the axes, $Z=24$

questions.question: Maximize $Z=-x_1-2x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\geq3$, $-x_1+x_2\leq1$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$; the feasible region of this linear program is unbounded. Which outcome does it have?
options: It is unbounded, because its feasible region is unbounded.
Infinitely many optimal solutions, on the edge where $x_1+x_2=3$.
Exactly one, the corner $(1,2)$ where both constraints bind, with $Z=-5$.
Exactly one optimal solution, $(3,0)$, with $Z=-3$.

questions.question: A linear program has infinitely many optimal solutions. Which statement about its optimal feasible corner points is correct?
options: If it has a feasible corner point, at least two of them are optimal, the ends of an optimal edge.
At least one of them is optimal, since an optimal solution is always attained at a feasible corner point.
If it has a feasible corner point, at least one of them is optimal, but possibly only one.
If it has a feasible corner point, none need be optimal, since only a unique optimum must be a corner point.

questions.question: A linear program $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ has an optimal solution, with optimal value $z^*$. One extra linear constraint is added and nothing else changes. Which outcomes are possible for the new linear program?
options: Only an optimal solution, with value at most $z^*$, since the extra constraint leaves the region nonempty.
Infeasible, unbounded or an optimal solution, since an extra constraint can change the region in any way.
Infeasible, or an optimal solution whose value is still exactly $z^*$, since the old optimum stays optimal.
Infeasible, or an optimal solution with value at most $z^*$; it can never become unbounded.

questions.question: For a real parameter $k$, maximize $Z=x_1+kx_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq4$, $x_1\leq3$, $x_1,x_2\geq0$. For which values of $k$ does this linear program have infinitely many optimal solutions?
options: For $k=1$ only
For $0\leq k\leq1$
For $k\leq0$ and for $k=1$

questions.question: Maximize $Z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2$ subject to $2x_1-x_2\leq4$, $-4x_1+2x_2\leq2$, with $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}$ and no domain definitions. For which $(c_1,c_2)$ does this linear program have an optimal solution, and how many optimal solutions are there then?
options: For $(c_1,c_2)=\lambda(2,-1)$ with $\lambda>0$ only; then exactly one
For $(c_1,c_2)=\lambda(2,-1)$ with any real $\lambda$; then infinitely many
For every $(c_1,c_2)$, as the region lies between two parallel lines; infinitely many
For all $c_1>0$ and $c_2<0$; then infinitely many, on the line $2x_1-x_2=4$
